lines.text: The Skeld don't call it the Pale. They call it the White. On the first morning, I understood why.
The trees were made of ice. Not covered in it. Made of it. You could see green leaves inside them, frozen in the middle of some summer nobody remembered.
Fascinating. Truly fascinating.
Ilse said fascinating eleven times that morning. By noon, her spectacles had frozen to her nose.
My lord. Look at your feet.
Wherever I stepped, the snow melted. A path of wet black earth followed me through the white, steaming a little, like bread fresh from the oven.
By afternoon, all eleven of us were walking in single file, exactly in my footprints. Even the dog.
Best I've felt in a week. Can we keep him, Wren?
He's the lord, Dunn.
Can we keep him anyway?
At night I lay awake and felt the threads. A hundred and twelve of them, running south. Every mile north, they stretched a little thinner.
Not weaker. Just further away. Like voices from another room.
You are listening to your people. Skeld mothers make that face when their children are out on the ice.
On the third day, Ilse took Dunn's stitches out. Underneath, the wound had closed into a thin pink line. Ilse said it should have taken a month.
Look at that! Good as new. Almost. Mostly. Ow.
That afternoon we crossed a frozen lake. Halfway over, Kell stopped dead.
Down. Everyone, down. Don't move. Don't breathe.
Under the ice, something was moving. A shadow. Long, and pale, and slow.
It passed beneath us for a very long time. The ice was melting under my hands, and I prayed that whatever it was couldn't feel warm.
When it was gone, nobody spoke for an hour.
...Can we go home now?
The oldest thing in the White. We do not say its name.
Tomorrow we reach a hunter's camp. A southerner's. He went into the White five winters ago, and never came back for it.
...Whose camp?
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter thirty-one, coming soon.
